The Collected Works shapes a civic brand identity for electric shuttle service Circuit with Stadt type, transit arrows, and fleet wraps.

Fifty cities meant fifty slightly different versions of Circuit. Founded by Alexander Esposito and James Mirras in the Hamptons in 2011, the electric shuttle service has logged over 10 million short neighborhood rides. Local tweaks gave early markets personality, yet the patchwork look left fleets reading like separate pilot programs instead of one operator. Strategy uncovered who really held the keys. Riders hail the cars, sure, but city officials and transit departments sign the contracts. Partner and Creative Director Justin Colt states New York and New Orleans studio The Collected Works stopped treating Circuit like a noisy startup. Instead, his team looked to everyday utilities like plumbing, gas, and electricity â public systems people expect to work.

Tossing out the archive wasnât necessary. Coltâs team sharpened Circuitâs original C icon, keeping its nested street grid and directional path intact. Every market name now locks beside the wordmark the exact same way, as seen on the dark Circuit Austin pill over an Airport Blvd highway interchange. Typography handles the daily workload across dozens of markets. Public Typeâs Stadt brings sharp thick-to-thin stroke contrast to headlines alongside Displaayâs Haffer, taking cues from the Fresh York City subway style guide. Thin map arrows sit right between words. On the metallic green rear fender wrap, hairline turn glyphs thread through âSay bye to circling the block.â Nearby touchpoints stay hyper-local: a tiled Brooklyn subway poster stacks âFrom Union Pool To Your Friends Roofâ in mint type, while a blue Boston brick mural pokes fun at Green Line delays.

It has been revealed that look at the dark green âWe Make the Short Trips Count.â billboard and another layer of this brand identity clicks. Wide sage-green bands with rounded street-corner turns cut straight across the display type. To keep that continuous Circuit line moving like a live route that doesnât repeat twice, the studio built a generative tool for in-house designers, paired with road-sign photo masks and snapping headline loops. Restraint matters most on the fleet wraps. Neighbors see the same shuttles parked three feet away or passing at 30 miles an hour for years. Deep green bodywork and a clean wordmark handle the 30-mph glance, while smaller fender copy and the dark-mapped rider app reward anyone standing at the curb.

#23017. Latest Update: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1546 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this upcoming generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app owners to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this upcoming generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

According to recent reports, perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user notes they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

Recent findings suggest that if the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

It has been revealed that I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

According to recent reports, an alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • According to recent reports, that’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • Sources indicate that none of this is easy, of course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

According to recent reports, that’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science highlights this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

Sources indicate that none of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

It has been revealed that Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he claims he doesn’t care. What should I do?

According to recent reports, A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” states Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Recent findings suggest that not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

It has been revealed that to help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

Industry observers note that “While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more promptly identify a purposeful direction.”.

Research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, says Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a massive challenge.

Sources indicate that instead of trying to manage their path, states Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

Industry observers note that “This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she claims. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Recent findings suggest that finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” indicates Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

Industry observers note that Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

“I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” indicates Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” claims Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, spending time with family is also notable. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

Only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an glitch, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

Recent findings suggest that one last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, says Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

The evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, says Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

That noted, it’s still notable for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Industry observers note that Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

According to recent reports, A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, claims Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

Sources indicate that as Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, notes Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

Sources indicate that if sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” says Farber. “It helps people find a new narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, indicates Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

Industry observers note that to help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, says Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

And as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” says Bibby.

According to recent reports, Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

Industry observers note that people turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, indicates Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

In her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

Read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

It has been revealed that to that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is newly introduced to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

According to recent reports, it also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Sources indicate that most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin says.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in Newly introduced York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

It has been revealed that women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, stated:.

“It’s a small change with the potential for a massive impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the Stanford Center on Longevity introduced in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that new and unprecedented reality.

Sources indicate that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

Sources indicate that in 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

Industry observers note that I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

Recent findings suggest that KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the Fresh Map of Life. What are you seeing?

Industry observers note that LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act rapidly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and said, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”.

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the New Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

It has been revealed that LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot rapidly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering new products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

Sources indicate that KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

In a recent development, it’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

According to recent reports, LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”.

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

Sources indicate that we have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

Tech Report: Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me.
  • Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors.
  • For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

In a recent development, at Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

Industry observers note that at Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Recent findings suggest that back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

In a recent development, it’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins notes these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”.

Sources indicate that mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Recent findings suggest that mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something new. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It has been revealed that it was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty.

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

According to recent reports, as I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In a recent development, in our Dickinson College episode, that choice indicates up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur.

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

Recent findings suggest that at Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones.

It has been revealed that in my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

Sources indicate that when Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang.

In a recent development, working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

Sources indicate that for example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III.

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It highlights that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Recent findings suggest that iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Sources indicate that logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco.

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

Recent findings suggest that as another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

Breaking: How Lead Exposure Erodes Long-Term Memory

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation.
  • In a recent development, environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains.
  • Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation. The study reveals that lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the de novo protein synthesis needed to consolidate lasting memories, while showing that targeted antioxidants can restore memory function in fruit fly models.

Source: China Medical University.

In a recent development, environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains. Yet despite decades of clinical observation, the precise molecular chain reaction through which lead disrupts memory storage inside individual neurons has remained elusive.

Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.

Published online on November 4, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study demonstrates that lead exposure hijacks mitochondrial redox homeostasis inside memory-consolidation neurons, starving the cell of the newly synthesized proteins required to lock short-term experiences into long-term memory.

To dissect how lead alters neural circuits without the confounding variables of mammalian systemic toxicity, the team turned to the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a premier model organism whose memory-encoding circuits are mapped down to single identified neurons.

Behavioral assays revealed a striking dissociation:.

To observe what occurs inside the brain during memory consolidation, the researchers deployed genetically encoded redox biosensors paired with live fluorescence microscopy.

It has been revealed that the imaging pinpointed a pair of dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, cells previously established by Chiang’s group as critical hubs for translating newly synthesized proteins during long-term memory formation. Within these DAL neurons, lead exposure severely disrupted redox homeostasis, tipping mitochondrial oxidation-reduction reactions into acute oxidative stress.

Recent findings suggest that this mitochondrial redox imbalance directly suppressed de novo protein synthesis within the DAL neurons. Without fresh structural and synaptic proteins to remodel neural connections, newly formed memories failed to consolidate.

To verify whether mitochondrial oxidative stress was the primary driver of memory loss, and whether the deficit could be reversed, the investigators administered several antioxidant compounds to lead-exposed flies, including N-acetylcysteine (NAC), astaxanthin, resveratrol, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major catechin found in green tea.

In a recent development, under controlled experimental conditions, these antioxidants significantly improved long-term memory performance. Deeper cellular imaging confirmed that EGCG reduced mitochondrial oxidative imbalance and restored normal protein synthesis inside the DAL neurons. Furthermore, administering either EGCG or the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO after a period of lead exposure restored the flies’ ability to form newly introduced long-term memories.

In a recent development, the authors emphasize that while these results demonstrate functional reversibility in fruit flies, they do not show the recovery of previously lost memories, nor do they establish that green tea or over-the-counter supplements can treat human lead poisoning. Further mammalian and clinical studies are necessary to determine whether targeting mitochondrial redox pathways can protect human cognition against heavy metal neurotoxicity.

How does lead exposure specifically affect memory?

In fruit fly experiments, researchers found that lead does not impair immediate learning or short-term memory. Instead, it selectively blocks the consolidation of long-term memories by preventing neurons from manufacturing the new proteins needed to stabilize those memories.

What role do mitochondria play in lead-induced memory loss?

Mitochondria regulate cellular energy and oxidation-reduction (redox) balance. Lead causes oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of memory-consolidation neurons (specifically DAL neurons), which shuts down local protein synthesis and prevents long-term memory storage.

Can antioxidants reverse memory damage caused by lead?

In the fruit fly study, antioxidants such as EGCG (found in green tea), NAC, resveratrol, and mitochondria-targeted MitoTEMPO reduced mitochondrial stress, restored neuronal protein synthesis, and allowed lead-exposed flies to form upcoming long-term memories. However, researchers caution that more studies are needed before applying these findings to humans.

Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila.

Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood.

Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms.

Industry observers note that using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation.

Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation.

Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
  • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
  • When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gretel rebuilt the Philadelphia Museum of Art brand identity around a revived griffin, custom Fairmount Serif and Philly street type.

The badge does the heavy lifting. A black roundel holds a white griffin, redrawn from the museum's 1938 original, with the institution's name set around it in sturdy capitals. The griffin is no invention: several of them sit on the museum's cornices, and merch carrying the old Griffy was already among the museum's best sellers. Gretel unveiled the identity on October 8, 2025, when the museum reintroduced itself under a shortened name; in February 2026 the museum restored its full name and kept the griffin. The brief was to come down the steps and throw the doors wide open, and the work answers with two registers at once: a quiet, refined institution and loud, vernacular programming.

In a recent development, the type tells the same story in two voices. Fairmount Serif is the museum's newly introduced custom institutional face, drawn with Ryan Bugden. It merges the museum's origins as the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Arts with Philadelphia's working-class heritage, taking serif details from the original seal and the engraved lettering on the museum walls. The research led Gretel to Hess Neobold, a twentieth-century American face cut by Sol Hess, a Philadelphia-born designer who studied at the museum's own school and later succeeded Frederic Goudy at Lanston Monotype.

Recent findings suggest that alongside it sits a vernacular library, a curated suite of typefaces borrowed from the city's storefronts, restaurants, murals and street vendors. The library is built to grow, with new custom faces commissioned for flagship exhibitions, so the loud register of the brand keeps changing while Fairmount Serif holds the center.

In a recent development, the system runs across every surface the museum owns. Wayfinding sets giant floor numerals in the stairwell and plain directional signs against the stone walls, while the parking cube carries the roundel over a single WELCOME. Tickets, wristbands, maps and membership cards repeat the same moves at hand scale: significant type, small badge, one color at a time. Enamel pins turn the griffin into a keepsake in black, white and pink.

The same logic scales up to the Great Stair Hall, where banners read Linger Longer, Come One Come All and This Is Your Museum, and out to exhibition books and rack cards that let each show pick its own vernacular voice. A digital overhaul with Gone Fishing and Self Aware rebuilt the web experience the same way. Photography by CoCo Hubbeling and Rob Cusick keeps the work grounded in the building.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research demonstrates that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a systemic condition influencing respiratory patterns, subjective time pressure, brain iron levels, and alcohol use risk across the lifespan. Together, these findings reveal distinct physiological and neural signatures that extend well beyond traditional behavioral symptoms.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Affecting approximately one in nine children in the United States, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions of childhood. While clinical assessments have historically focused on hallmark behavioral traits, inattention, impulsivity, and motor hyperactivity, mounting evidence indicates that ADHD exerts far-reaching effects on physical and mental health well into adulthood.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four upcoming studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.

Taken together, the emerging findings map distinct physiological and behavioral signatures across development:.

By connecting autonomic physiology, neurochemistry, and lived cognitive stress, these studies challenge narrow definitions of ADHD as purely an attentional or behavioral disorder.

“It is becoming clear that ADHD is a broader systemic condition affecting a host of brain and body variables beyond just motor hyperactivity,” noted press conference moderator Dr. Chandan Vaidya, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University who studies how regulatory behavior goes awry in neurodevelopmental conditions. “Together, these new findings tackle timely topics and showcase the diversity of areas where work is needed to better understand ADHD and ultimately improve diagnosis and treatment.”.

How does ADHD affect physical functions outside of attention and hyperactivity?

Upcoming research presented at Neuroscience 2026 reveals that ADHD is linked to distinct breathing patterns in young adults, lower iron levels in specific regions of the developing brain, and chronic psychological time pressure, demonstrating that the condition involves both brain-wide neurochemistry and bodily physiology.

What did researchers discover about brain iron in children with ADHD?

Sources indicate that brain scans conducted by researchers at UC San Diego revealed that children and adolescents with ADHD have lower levels of iron in specific brain regions compared to peers without ADHD. Because iron is crucial for producing neurotransmitters like dopamine, tracking these regional changes may offer latest insights into ADHD neurobiology.

Can treating ADHD help reduce alcohol misuse in young adults?

Yes. Emerging clinical data from the University of Florida indicates that ADHD medication may help decrease problem drinking behaviors among young adults who experience both ADHD and alcohol use disorder.

#23006. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1670 w)
