You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent.
  • It has been revealed that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves.
  • Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It has been revealed that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a upcoming paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”.

According to recent reports, these people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

In a recent development, if you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”.

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”.

Sources indicate that rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Recent findings suggest that some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another noted, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”.

Rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person noted, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”.

It’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person stated.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”.

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly notable for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”.

According to recent reports, naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

Recent findings suggest that one participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”.

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

Recent findings suggest that they may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once remarked, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

Sources indicate that for organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

In a recent development, that is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Neurosciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Scent and Memory: Why Novelty Boosts Recall in Older Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults.
  • The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus.
  • However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults. unless it is experienced as a novel cue at the very start of learning. The findings show that older adults who encountered the scent during the initial learning block recalled objects significantly better, highlighting how sensory novelty and intact smell function support cognitive aging.

The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus. Because a single familiar whiff can trigger vivid autobiographical flashbacks, aromatherapy, particularly using lavender essential oil, has frequently been touted as a simple tool to sharpen memory and stave off age-related cognitive decline.

However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.

Now, a study published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience by neuroscientists at UCLA and Rice University reveals that the relationship between scent and memory depends heavily on timing, sensory novelty, and baseline olfactory health.

Recent findings suggest that led by UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Dr. Stephanie Leal, the investigation highlights that while lavender scent alone did not act as a blanket memory booster, encountering the scent as a fresh, novel stimulus at the beginning of a learning session significantly enhanced recall in older adults.

Because age-related olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease, Leal and colleagues set out to examine how olfactory cues interact with memory encoding in cognitively healthy younger and older adults.

Sources indicate that participants first completed standardized olfactory assessments to measure baseline smell sensitivity before entering either a room diffused with lavender essential oil or an unscented room. Volunteers viewed two sequential blocks of everyday household objects, such as a tomato or a blow dryer, on a computer screen. Crucially, the design was counterbalanced: participants who experienced the lavender scent during the first image block completed the second block in an unscented room, and vice versa.

Following a delay, participants underwent a nuanced memory test featuring images that were either identical to, slightly altered from (e.g., changing a red blow dryer to blue), or completely different from the original items. This paradigm allowed researchers to separate general recall (recognizing the object category) from high-resolution detail memory (remembering exact visual features).

“When we looked at general and detail memory measures, older adults struggled to remember the details, which we expected,” explained Leal. “Interestingly, the presence or absence of odor made no difference for older or younger adults. We were kind of scratching our heads because that was surprising based on prior work that revealed olfaction might enhance memory.”.

A deeper look at the experimental order, however, uncovered a striking pattern among older adults:.

These results suggest that as the brain ages, the specific chemical profile of an essential oil matters far less than the novelty of encountering an enriched sensory environment at the onset of learning.

Rather than treating aromatherapy as a passive background cure-all, the findings indicate that olfactory cues work best when deployed strategically to introduce novelty during newly introduced learning experiences.

“If we want to support memory in older adults, we need to think beyond simply whether a stimulus helps or hurts memory and consider when and how it is experienced,” Leal noted. “A big component of learning in aging is novelty. Engaging in learning in an enriched context may make it easier to learn upcoming things.”.

By linking baseline smell sensitivity, subjective pleasantness, and timed sensory novelty to hippocampal memory precision, the research offers practical insights for designing enriched cognitive interventions aimed at supporting healthy brain aging.

Does diffusing lavender essential oil automatically improve memory?

No. Researchers at UCLA and Rice University found that overall, both younger and older adults performed no better on memory tests in a lavender-scented room compared to an unscented room.

Why did encountering the scent first help older adults remember better?

Older adults who smelled lavender during the very first learning block recalled objects more accurately than those exposed during the second block. This suggests that the novelty of entering an enriched sensory environment at the start of a task helps the aging brain anchor fresh memories.

How does sense of smell connect to Alzheimer’s disease and aging?

Sources indicate that age-related loss of smell is closely linked to early neurodegenerative changes in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, older adults with healthier baseline olfactory function, and those who found the scent pleasant, revealed better detail memory, highlighting the close tie between olfactory processing and hippocampal memory circuits.

Funding: The researchers involved in this project were funded by the National Science Foundation, the BrightFocus Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Alzheimer’s Association.

Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.

Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus.

Recent findings suggest that age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination.

In the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test.

Across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults.

However, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability.

These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.

Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken.
  • Throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography.
  • Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

Throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN revealed pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

Industry observers note that circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

Recent findings suggest that researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Funding: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers JP21K19287, JP21H05036, JP23H04941, and JP22K21351); AMED (grant number JP21zf0127005); JST CREST (grant number JPMJCR24T4); JST SPRING (grant number JPMJSP2124) and the World Premier International Research Center Initiative (WPI).

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

Sources indicate that the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but showed reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain.
  • Biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously.
  • In a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study highlights that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

In a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

“Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

Researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

In a recent development, no. The study indicates that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

In a recent development, taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

According to recent reports, acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.

Brain Computes Motion Direction Independently From the Eye

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently.
  • Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.
  • For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently. The study mapped nearly 46,000 mouse brain cells to uncover a dual visual system in the superior colliculus, separating localized object tracking from global self-motion sensing.

Source: UC San Francisco / Nature.

Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.

For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.

Sources indicate that because these retinal ganglion cells already encode directional vectors, researchers widely assumed the brain simply inherited that pre-calculated motion data passively from the eye. However, no mapping technology existed that could simultaneously trace exact synaptic connections from the retina while identifying the molecular identity of every receiving brain cell.

Now, in a study published in Nature, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) have bridged that technological gap.

Led by co-senior authors Dr. Xin Duan, professor of ophthalmology, and Dr. Evan Feinberg, professor of anatomy, alongside postdoctoral fellow Dr. Fei Wang, the team built a scalable eye-to-brain wiring atlas revealing that specialized circuits in the midbrain compute motion direction completely on their own.

Over the past decade, Duan’s laboratory pioneered anterograde trans-neuronal tracing, a technique in which a fluorescent molecular tracer delivered to the eye crosses synaptic junctions to illuminate only those downstream brain neurons directly receiving retinal input.

To scale this tool from single-circuit tracing into a comprehensive atlas, Wang paired the trans-neuronal tracer with MERFISH (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization), a spatial transcriptomic method that reads gene activity across thousands of individual cells in a tissue slice simultaneously to pinpoint each neuron’s exact genetic identity.

Applying this combined platform across nearly 46,000 cells in the mouse visual system, the investigators uncovered hundreds of distinct retinal-to-brain connection pairs.

“It’s like an entire atlas we’ve built,” Wang said. “We’ve uncovered hundreds of pairs of connections between the eye and the brain. We ended up focusing on only one page of this atlas, but there are many left to study in the future.”.

Focusing on the superior colliculus, an evolutionarily conserved midbrain hub essential for visual orientation and rapid motor reflexes, Wang, Feinberg, and Duan recorded real-time neural firing while showing mice high-contrast black bars scrolling across a screen in eight distinct directions.

Combining functional recordings with their molecular wiring map exposed two separate motion-processing architectures operating side by side:.

Sources indicate that “We think these sets of cells are doing slightly different things from each other,” Wang explained. “The eye cells detecting direction may specialize in small, local motions like prey or food. The brain cells computing direction sense a larger background movement.”.

The investigators hypothesize that this global background motion signal informs an organism of its own self-motion and spatial trajectory as it navigates through the environment.

Beyond resolving a foundational question in visual neuroscience, the high-resolution wiring atlas carries direct translational implications for regenerative medicine and neuroengineering. As researchers advance toward optic nerve regeneration, whole-eye transplantation, and high-resolution visual brain-machine interfaces for patients with glaucoma, trauma, or multiple sclerosis, restoring functional sight requires reconnecting damaged axons to their exact functional targets.

“This is a fundamental mechanism that has been understudied from a basic science perspective, but it also has applied value,” said Duan. “If we ever want to repair or restore vision in people, we need to know which neural connections need to be rewired for functional vision.”.

“In addition to providing a blueprint for revealing structural maps of the brain, our study illustrates how the resulting maps can be used to answer longstanding questions regarding brain function,” added Feinberg.

The team notes that their scalable tracer-plus-MERFISH platform can be adapted to map how the eye regulates circadian rhythms, and generalized to chart cell-to-cell connectivity across any organ system in the body.

Does the eye do all the work of detecting which way things move?

No. While specialized cells in the retina detect motion direction and send that data to the brain, UCSF researchers discovered a second group of neurons in the brain’s superior colliculus that independently calculates motion direction using basic visual inputs, even when the eye’s own direction-sensing cells are turned off.

Why does the brain have two different systems for sensing motion?

Researchers believe the two pathways handle different visual jobs: the eye’s direction-sensing cells appear specialized for tracking small, local moving targets (like food, prey, or a flying ball), while the brain’s independent motion-computing cells detect large-scale background movement to help track how your own body is moving through space.

How could this brain-mapping tool help restore vision in the future?

In a recent development, to successfully develop eye transplants, optic nerve repairs, or visual brain-machine interfaces for conditions like glaucoma or multiple sclerosis, scientists need an exact wiring diagram showing which eye cells connect to which functional brain circuits. This newly introduced atlas provides that precise rewiring blueprint.

TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.

It has been revealed that A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types.

Recent findings suggest that here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry) with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)) to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution.

These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses.

Sources indicate that we validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC.

Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

Sources indicate that according to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, stated, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”.

In a recent development, homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who right now serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”.

According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study demonstrates Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

It has been revealed that one former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”.

The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.

This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

UC Berkeley School of Public Health has been a global health leader in research innovation, educational excellence, and social impact for more than 75 years.

Ultraprocessed Foods Alter Food-Reward Brain Activity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected.
  • Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States.
  • In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected. The fMRI study indicates blunted activation in the developing orbitofrontal cortex, a key region for food valuation and self-control, even when diets are strictly matched for calories, sugar, fat, and nutrients.

Source: Virginia Tech / Obesity.

Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States. While extensive research links these foods to obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease, neuroscientists are increasingly uncovering how industrial processing directly interacts with the developing human brain.

In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.

Led by first author Dr. Emma Leslie alongside neuroscientist Dr. Alex DiFeliceantonio and registered dietitian Dr. Brenda Davy, the findings complement earlier results from the same trial showing that 18- to 21-year-olds consumed excess calories at a buffet meal after eating ultraprocessed foods, even when they were no longer hungry.

Recent findings suggest that to separate the effects of industrial food processing from basic nutritional content, the researchers recruited 22 healthy adults ages 18 to 25 (including seven participants ages 21 or younger) for a randomized crossover feeding trial. Each participant followed two strictly controlled diets for two weeks apiece, separated by a four-week washout period:.

Critically, both diets were engineered to have identical macronutrient profiles (50% carbohydrates, 35% fat, 15% protein), matching levels of fiber, added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality, calibrated to keep each participant’s body weight stable.

Before and after each two-week dietary phase, participants underwent functional MRI (fMRI) brain scans while receiving small sips of an ultraprocessed milkshake or a tasteless control solution through a specialized delivery tube.

When the researchers analyzed the neuroimaging data, they discovered a striking developmental divide:.

“Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” explained Leslie, who conducted the work as a doctoral student at Virginia Tech and is now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan.

Industry observers note that located just behind the eyes, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the final regions of the human brain to finish maturing, continuing to remodel into the mid- to late 20s. It plays a central role in evaluating food rewards, regulating cravings, and exerting executive self-control to stop eating.

Because the two diets were matched across nutritional metrics, the findings point toward non-nutritive properties of ultraprocessed foods, such as chemical additives, emulsifiers, texture alterations, or compounds generated during industrial processing, as potential drivers of altered brain signaling.

It has been revealed that “This study is important because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” said DiFeliceantonio, associate professor at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute and interim co-director of its Center for Health Behaviors Research. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”.

While the researchers note that the sample size was small and the age-based findings were exploratory, and did not directly correlate individual fMRI shifts with buffet calorie intake, the results highlight adolescence and early adulthood as critical windows of neurodevelopmental sensitivity.

Sources indicate that next, DiFeliceantonio and Davy plan to investigate whether adolescents under 18, who consume the highest proportion of ultraprocessed foods of any U.S. demographic, show even stronger neural sensitivity, and whether brain responses recover once individuals return to whole-food diets.

How do ultraprocessed foods affect the brains of young adults?

A Virginia Tech study found that after eating a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks, young adults ages 18 to 21 showed decreased brain activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in food reward, valuation, and self-control, when tasting a milkshake. Adults ages 22 to 25 did not show these brain changes.

Was the brain effect simply caused by extra sugar, fat, or calories?

No. Both the ultraprocessed diet and the unprocessed comparison diet contained the exact same amounts of calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein, added sugars, saturated fat, fiber, and sodium. This suggests that industrial food processing or additives themselves, rather than basic nutrients, drove the brain changes.

Why are 18- to 21-year-olds more sensitive to ultraprocessed foods than slightly older adults?

According to recent reports, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish developing, continuing to mature into the mid- to late 20s. Because this self-control and reward-evaluation circuit is still actively wiring in 18- to 21-year-olds, it appears more sensitive to dietary shifts.

Funding: The research was supported by a grant to DiFeliceantonio and Davy from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, part of the National Institutes of Health. Leslie was also supported with an exercise health sciences graduate fellowship from Dr. Ray A. Gaskins.

It has been revealed that the average American consumes 55% of daily energy from ultraprocessed foods (UPF), created through industrial processes and additives not used at home. We investigated if a high-UPF diet alters brain response to milkshake compared with a diet free from UPF in emerging adults, who are in a critical brain development period and typically consume high amounts of UPF.

It has been revealed that in a randomized controlled crossover trial participants aged 18–25 years completed two 2-week controlled feeding periods including a UPF (81% UPF) and non-UPF (0% UPF) diet. Before and after each diet intervention, participants consumed milkshake concomitant with functional magnetic resonance imaging.

Sources indicate that in the entire cohort, there were no differences between diet conditions in brain response. An exploratory analysis revealed orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake decreased after the UPF diet and increased following the non-UPF diet in late adolescents (18–21 years) but not young adults (22–25 years). In all participants, habitual UPF intake (g) was positively associated with orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake, independent of diet condition.

It has been revealed that an acute UPF dietary intervention may only alter brain response in late adolescents. Further work is needed to determine potential vulnerability of late adolescents to changes in dietary UPF on brain response to rewards.

ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05550818.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012.
  • Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.
  • In a recent development, over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012. The analysis of over 35,000 participants indicates that rising youth anxiety reflects genuine shifts in psychological distress rather than mere mental health awareness.

Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

In a recent development, over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America. Yet clinicians and epidemiologists have hotly debated a central question: does this statistical surge reflect a true rise in underlying psychological distress, or are young people simply more familiar with clinical terminology and more willing to report symptoms?

Newly introduced research led by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and Boston University School of Public Health provides compelling evidence that underlying cognitive vulnerability is genuinely intensifying.

Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study tracks three decades of data on intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—a foundational psychological mechanism characterized by acute distress when facing ambiguous situations, missing information, or unpredictable outcomes.

Analyzing data from more than 35,000 college students in the United States and Canada between 1992 and 2023, the researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty increased steadily over 30 years—and accelerated dramatically around 2012, growing roughly three times faster over the past decade than during the 1990s and 2000s.

It has been revealed that to track population-level shifts in how young adults tolerate ambiguity, first author Dr. Jeroen M. Van Baar, postdoctoral associate in epidemiology at Boston University School of Public Health, and senior author Dr. Katherine M. Keyes, professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, conducted a systematic temporal meta-analysis using the Web of Science database.

Recent findings suggest that after screening nearly 300 full-text peer-reviewed studies published between 2007 and 2025, the team synthesized data from 138 studies encompassing 35,296 college-aged participants across the U.S. and Canada who completed standardized 27-item or 12-item versions of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale.

Recent findings suggest that across the entire 31-year window from 1992 through 2023, average IU scores increased by approximately 0.65 points annually. Crucially, the trajectory bent sharply upward around 2012: between 2012 and 2023, intolerance of uncertainty rose at roughly triple the annual pace recorded between 1992 and 2011.

Industry observers note that “Our results provide updated insights into one of the core building blocks of anxiety: intolerance of uncertainty,” explained Keyes. “IU is not itself a health outcome or a root cause of disease, but an intermediary cognitive process that contributes to the development of anxiety.”.

For an individual with high intolerance of uncertainty, everyday unpredictability, such as attending a latest class without knowing every expectation or navigating an unstructured social event, can trigger disproportionate cognitive threat and emotional distress. Elevated IU is a well-established transdiagnostic risk factor linked to generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depression.

Crucially, because “intolerance of uncertainty” remains a specialized clinical metric largely unfamiliar outside psychology, it provides a vital safeguard against reporting bias.

“Some researchers have argued that increases in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms among young people may partly reflect greater mental health awareness,” noted Van Baar. “Because young people are now more familiar with terms like ‘anxiety’, they may be more likely to report symptoms in surveys even if their underlying feelings have not changed. On the other hand, intolerance of uncertainty remains a relatively unfamiliar concept outside psychology, making this study less vulnerable to that criticism.”.

“The fact that we observed a consistent increase in intolerance of uncertainty that mirrored trends in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms suggests these patterns are unlikely to be explained solely by greater mental health awareness and may instead reflect genuine changes in underlying mental health,” Keyes added.

While the study did not isolate a single environmental trigger, the authors point to a convergence of mutually reinforcing societal shifts—including the rapid adoption of smartphones and social media around 2012, escalating academic competition, rising loneliness, economic instability, childhood adversity, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that “It is likely that these factors are intertwined and mutually reinforcing, jointly contributing to population-level increases in intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety among young adults,” Van Baar remarked. “Any explanation will be strongest if it accounts for both the long-term upward trend since the 1990s and the inflection point observed around 2012.”.

Recent findings suggest that despite the sobering trajectory, the researchers emphasize a clear path forward: unlike broad macroeconomic forces, intolerance of uncertainty is a modifiable cognitive habit. Targeted cognitive-behavioral therapies specifically designed to build tolerance for ambiguity already exist, and scaling these interventions for young adults could help curb the youth anxiety crisis at its cognitive roots.

What is “intolerance of uncertainty,” and how does it relate to anxiety?

Industry observers note that intolerance of uncertainty is a psychological tendency to feel distressed, overwhelmed, or threatened when facing unpredictable outcomes or missing information. It acts as a core cognitive building block that significantly increases a person’s vulnerability to developing anxiety and mood disorders.

How much has intolerance of uncertainty increased among college students?

Analyzing data from 35,296 U.S. and Canadian college students between 1992 and 2023, researchers found that scores rose steadily by about 0.65 points per year, and accelerated three times faster between 2012 and 2023 compared to the previous two decades.

Does this prove rising youth anxiety isn’t just due to greater mental health awareness?

It has been revealed that yes, it provides strong evidence against the “awareness-only” theory. Because “intolerance of uncertainty” is a specialized psychological concept rather than an everyday term young people use to self-label, its steep rise mirrors anxiety trends without being skewed by changing vocabulary or awareness.

Funding: The study was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, grant 5T32MH013043.The authors have no financial conflicts of interest to declare.

Intolerance of Uncertainty among U.S. and Canadian Young Adults Attending College 1992-2023: A Meta-analysis.

Rising anxiety prevalence among young adults may relate to intolerance of uncertainty (IU), difficulty enduring the perceived absence of notable information. A prior meta-analysis found increasing long-form Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS) scores among US and Canadian undergraduates from 1992 to 2014, but recent evidence is lacking.

To estimate IU trends among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023 by extending the prior meta-analysis and including the short-form IUS.

Web of Science was used to track English-language articles from Canada or the US citing the source articles for the long-form or short-form IUS across 13 databases.

Eligible studies were peer-reviewed empirical articles with nonclinical undergraduate samples from the US or Canada that reported sample size and mean long-form or short-form IUS.

According to recent reports, following MOOSE guidelines, 2 investigators extracted study characteristics and mean IU, resolving discrepancies jointly. Studies were merged with the prior meta-analysis and analyzed using fixed-effect meta-regression. To assess IU across scale forms, mean IU was converted into SD units and regressed onto data collection year, weighted by sample size, and adjusted for mean age and sex or gender distribution. Study data were analyzed from September 2025 to July 2026.

According to recent reports, mean IU. The hypothesis was preregistered before data collection.

Recent findings suggest that of 799 abstracts screened and 294 full texts reviewed independently by 2 investigators, 92 articles (11%) met selection criteria. After merger with prior meta-analysis and removal of duplicates, this meta-analysis included 137 studies (62 long-form IUS and 75 short-form IUS) comprising 37 298 participants (unweighted median [IQR] of sample mean age, 20.1 [19.4-21.3] years; 69.5% female [unweighted mean of sample sex/gender distribution]). Mean long-form IU increased from 1992 to 2023 by 0.66 points annually (95% CI, 0.47-0.84 points) on a scale from 27 to 135. Mean short-form IU increased from 2005 (first sample) to 2023 by 0.60 points annually (95% CI, 0.43-0.76 points) on a scale from 12 to 60. In the combined sample, mean IU grew by 0.04 SD per year from 1992 to 2023 (95% CI, 0.03-0.05 SD per year), with 3-fold faster growth during 2012-2023 (0.06 SD per year; 95% CI, 0.04-0.08 SD per year) than during 1992-2011 (0.02 SD per year; 95% CI, 0-0.04 SD per year).

Results of this meta-analysis suggest that IU increased among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023, with a steeper increase after 2012. This supports further investigating the role of uncertainty in the epidemiology of anxiety.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts revealed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results revealed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.
