#22972. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life.
  • According to recent reports, the study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India.
  • Industry observers note that superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

According to recent reports, the study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

The Brain's Local Communication Network.

Industry observers note that superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

Recent findings suggest that "Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," remarked Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it.".

Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring.

To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

The researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss.

In a recent development, measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

When these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," said Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition.".

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations.

It has been revealed that the researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

In a recent development, the researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

What Scientists Still Need to Learn.

Sources indicate that because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

According to recent reports, "A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," remarked Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan.".

In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#22971. Breaking: How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • It has been revealed that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

It has been revealed that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

Recent findings suggest that so I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious intends produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Sources indicate that repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

Success is motivating. Doing what you stated you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a substantial part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate intends but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Industry observers note that micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Sources indicate that across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

Industry observers note that I hate the idea of abandoning my big aims. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Recent findings suggest that break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Industry observers note that then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Industry observers note that expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Industry observers note that every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

It has been revealed that at some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to abandon our grand prepares and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Industry observers note that christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#22970. Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older.
  • According to recent reports, the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues.
  • In a recent development, the researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older. Yet experiments in mice suggest that changes in a protein deep inside the brain can influence all three. Restoring that protein, called Menin, improved several signs of aging, while a separate treatment with the amino acid D-serine improved cognition.

According to recent reports, the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues. The work identified a possible connection between brain inflammation, metabolism, and aging throughout the body. Research published since then has added to that picture, while also showing why the supplement findings require careful interpretation.

How a Brain Protein Could Influence Aging.

In a recent development, the researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions. It also appears to influence how the body ages. As inflammatory signaling increases in this region, it can contribute to changes both within the brain and in tissues elsewhere in the body.

Sources indicate that before the 2023 study, Leng and colleagues had found that Menin helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. That raised an important question: Could losing some of this protection help set age-related decline in motion?

Recent findings suggest that the team found that Menin levels fell with age in certain neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus, an area involved in regulating metabolism. The same decline was not seen in astrocytes and microglia, two types of cells that support and protect the brain. This suggested that the change was specific to particular cells rather than a uniform loss across the region.

To investigate whether Menin loss could actually contribute to aging, rather than simply accompany it, the researchers created conditional knockout mice. These animals were genetically engineered so that Menin could be selectively removed. Reducing Menin in younger mice increased hypothalamic inflammation and brought on several aging-related traits, including lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and a modestly shorter lifespan.

Menin loss also disrupted a chemical pathway important for communication between brain cells. Mice with less Menin had lower levels of D-serine, an amino acid that helps activate receptors involved in learning and memory. These receptors help neurons adjust the strength of their connections, a process essential for storing information.

An enzyme involved in D-serine production (which was in turn regulated by Menin) became less active, reducing the amino acid's supply. The findings suggested that Menin could influence cognition not only through inflammation, but also by helping maintain the chemistry that supports brain signaling.

Sources indicate that D-serine is sometimes used as a dietary supplement, but an important distinction can get lost in discussions of food sources. Serine occurs in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts, while the form incorporated into dietary proteins is L-serine. The body can convert L-serine into D-serine, but the two forms are not interchangeable, and eating these foods is not equivalent to receiving the experimental D-serine treatment.

It has been revealed that the researchers next tested whether raising Menin levels could improve the condition of elderly (20-month-old) mice. They delivered the gene for Menin into the hypothalamus, allowing cells in that region to produce more of the protein.

Thirty days later, the treated mice had improvements in skin thickness and bone mass, along with better performance on tests of learning, cognition, and balance. The changes were accompanied by higher D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. The study also reported that restoring Menin extended lifespan in the treated mice.

A separate experiment tested a simpler approach: giving mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks. This improved cognitive performance, including in older animals. However, the supplement did not reproduce the broader improvements in physical aging traits seen after Menin restoration. The distinction matters: the study did not show that taking D-serine reversed aging throughout the body.

At the time, Leng described the potential significance of the findings:.

"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline.".

Leng added, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

Subsequent studies have explored related mechanisms, although they should not be treated as direct confirmation of the entire Menin aging pathway.

A study published in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry in March 2024 examined Menin in cultured mouse hippocampal cells exposed to the stress hormone corticosterone. A compound called itaconate increased Menin levels and reduced inflammation and a form of cell death. When the researchers silenced Menin, that protection disappeared. The result supported a protective role for Menin in another experimental setting, but it was a cell study, not a demonstration of slower aging in animals or people.

Recent findings suggest that other work has strengthened the case that communication between the hypothalamus and the rest of the body can influence aging. In a 2024 Cell Metabolism study, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. Interventions that maintained or stimulated this system increased physical activity and extended lifespan in mice. The study involved a different molecular pathway from Menin, but reinforced the broader idea that brain signals can affect aging beyond the brain.

Industry observers note that A much larger view emerged in January 2025, when an Allen Institute team reported an analysis of roughly 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature. Some of the cell types most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the hypothalamus's third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity. Many demonstrated reduced activity in genes associated with neuronal function alongside increased activity in genes related to immune responses. That study mapped changes associated with aging rather than testing a treatment, but it highlighted the hypothalamus as an vital area for further investigation.

Why More D-Serine Is Not Necessarily Better.

Later research also complicates the idea that increasing D-serine should always benefit an aging brain.

In April 2025, a study in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences examined mice engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease. In that model, an early rise in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Genetically removing the enzyme that produces D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive problems. This was a different biological setting from the Menin experiments, but it demonstrated that D-serine can have different effects depending on the underlying disease process.

Research published on September 16, 2026, in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease pointed in another direction. In a different Alzheimer's mouse model, a diet enriched with L-serine increased blood levels of both L-serine and D-serine and partially restored measures of latest neuron production in the hippocampus. It did not improve the buildup of amyloid, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, this experiment tested L-serine and the production of new neurons, not D-serine supplementation as a treatment for human aging.

Taken together, these findings suggest that serine metabolism is a promising research target, but not a simple case of more being better. The form of serine, the condition being studied, and the outcome being measured all matter. Neither study directly confirms or overturns the original Menin results.

What the Findings Mean for People.

There is some human research on D-serine, although it does not establish an aging treatment. A small randomized study published in 2016, before the Menin work, tested a single dose in 50 healthy older adults. Participants improved on one measure of a computerized maze task, but the researchers found no significant benefit on the other cognitive tests or mood measures. The experiment did not establish lasting memory benefits, slower aging, or the safety of prolonged use in older adults.

It has been revealed that the Menin findings leave several notable questions unresolved. Researchers still need to determine what causes the protein to decline with age, how much of the resulting physical and cognitive deterioration can be prevented, and how long any benefits might last. They also need to understand whether altering Menin or supplementing D-serine could produce unintended effects.

Sources indicate that the central possibility remains compelling: some changes associated with aging may be influenced by signals originating in a small part of the brain. Understanding those signals could reveal ways to protect function later in life. For now, however, the evidence points to an experimental pathway worth investigating, not a supplement proven to turn back human aging.

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
  • Industry observers note that researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels.
  • The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.

Industry observers note that researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.

The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.

A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research.

For now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.

Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.

In a recent development, postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, says one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.

It has been revealed that "Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The fresh implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," says Kunyang Sui.

Sources indicate that sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.

Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers.

Sources indicate that brain researchers currently use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.

Conventional fibers, however, have an notable limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.

How the Upcoming Brain Implant Works.

The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.

A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.

The finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be key because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.

According to recent reports, the researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.

The experiments showed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

They were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.

Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience.

According to recent reports, the in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.

Industry observers note that the research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.

#22966. Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time.
  • “We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski states.
  • It has been revealed that that changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski states.

It has been revealed that that changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

According to recent reports, “He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

Industry observers note that the Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” says Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

It has been revealed that surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

In a recent development, life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

Sources indicate that djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

“It is very important not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she says. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”.

It has been revealed that admitting your own lack of control over the major picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski says. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”.

According to recent reports, once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

“These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”.

It has been revealed that self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

Sources indicate that after Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly promptly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

In a recent development, “You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski claims. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”.

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

According to recent reports, “I simply try to live in the here and now and not to proposal,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”.

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

Industry observers note that as governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

Industry observers note that this helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

In a recent development, djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she says. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was new for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski indicates. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”.

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

Recent findings suggest that “Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” states Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a major reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

Sources indicate that when you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

Industry observers note that “To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski notes. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”.

It has been revealed that though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

It has been revealed that for the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most vital to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

It has been revealed that the couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski says. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”.

It has been revealed that some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski says. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”.

One unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

It has been revealed that military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

According to recent reports, djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

“This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Sources indicate that padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco says. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”.

In a recent development, elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

Industry News: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • It has been revealed that to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more important issue: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

It has been revealed that to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an important marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

"Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," says Prof. Kurpas.

Industry observers note that in practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

"The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

It has been revealed that another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

Industry observers note that "It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be vital," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

Caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

In that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

"If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," says Prof. Kurpas.

These findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

It has been revealed that "Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. Newly introduced research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

It has been revealed that different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.

It has been revealed that the researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

Industry observers note that to explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

Recent findings suggest that during the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions rapidly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

Recent findings suggest that if dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

It has been revealed that the idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

Recent findings suggest that "While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. New research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

Recent findings suggest that the new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

According to recent reports, the regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

Recent findings suggest that after coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Industry observers note that improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

It has been revealed that coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

According to recent reports, caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

It has been revealed that because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide newly introduced clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Sources indicate that corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," noted Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

#22962. Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1787 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward.
  • Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her newly introduced book, Artificial Intimacy.
  • While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create new jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her newly introduced book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

According to recent reports, with loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “firm” for the lonely?

In a recent development, the harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

It has been revealed that for example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

It has been revealed that while it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

It has been revealed that interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

Sources indicate that “For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Industry observers note that turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, claims Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Recent findings suggest that of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” notes Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”.

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

“If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our initiative, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”.

According to recent reports, turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

Recent findings suggest that for example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

“Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”.

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”.

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with newly introduced iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”.

Industry observers note that still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”.

According to recent reports, to this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

In a recent development, “We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

While her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is key for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”.

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#22960. Industry News: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (919 w)
